Astronomers just announced a new addition to the solar system's outer neighborhood, and it's a weird little guy. This candidate dwarf planet is a frozen world about 700 kilometers across, orbiting far beyond Neptune on a long, tilted path that takes it nearly 400 years to circle the Sun once. It was found by combing through survey images for faint dots that moved slowly against the background stars. Follow-up observations confirmed that it's real and not a glitch. What makes it exciting is its orbit; it's different enough from its neighbors that scientists think something may have nudged it there long ago. There's still a lot we don't know, including its color, its surface, and whether it has a moon. But it's another clue in the puzzle of how the outer solar system got its shape.
